I Wasted 98.5% of My Claude Tokens — Here Are 10 Fixes That Actually Work

Rohan Mistry

I burned through a $200 Claude plan in 2 hours. Here is the hidden “context tax” eating your budget — and how I cut it to near zero.

Every developer hitting Claude’s limit tells themselves the same story.

“The plan is too restrictive. I need to upgrade.”

I told myself that too. So I upgraded.

Hit the limit again — faster.

That’s when I stopped blaming Anthropic and started actually looking at where my tokens were going. What I found made me feel like an idiot.

Non-Member’s Link!

Here’s the problem nobody explains:

Claude doesn’t just read your latest message — it re-reads the entire conversation from scratch, every single turn.

Message Count | Tokens Read | Cost Multiplier
--------------|-------------|----------------
1             | 500         | 1x
10            | 6,000       | 12x
30            | 15,000      | 30x

Same question. 30x the price. Not a billing glitch. Not a broken plan. Just a compounding context window you didn’t know about.

These 10 fixes stopped the bleeding.

The 10 Token Drains — And How to Stop Them

  1. Long conversations compound like debt
  2. MCP servers add hidden overhead
  3. Flying blind without visibility tools
  4. Sending multiple messages when one would do
  5. Letting the model go down the wrong path
  6. Bloated instruction files that reload every turn
  7. Waiting too long to compact context
  8. Idle sessions killing your cache
  9. Running heavy tasks at the wrong time
  10. Using expensive models where cheaper ones would do

Token Drain #1 — Long Conversations Compound Like Debt

This is the one that explains everything else.

Claude doesn’t just read your latest message. It re-reads the entire conversation from the very beginning — every single turn. Think of it like a snowball rolling downhill.

Turn 1:   Claude reads   500 tokens
Turn 5:   Claude reads 3,500 tokens
Turn 10:  Claude reads 6,000 tokens
Turn 30:  Claude reads 15,000 tokens  ← same question, 30x the cost

By message 30, you’re paying 15,000 tokens for one reply — before you’ve typed a word.

I ran /cost after one of my own sessions. Here's the receipt:

Total tokens used:               142,000
Tokens spent re-reading history: 140,000
Tokens spent on actual code:       2,000

I wasn’t running out of tokens. I was wasting them.

The fix: Use /clear between unrelated tasks. Not at the end of the day. Between every task.

Power users don’t run one long session all day. They run ten short focused ones. One task. One context. Then clear.

It feels like losing progress. You’re not.

You’re losing cost.

“Claude isn’t forgetting. It’s re-reading. Every time.”

Token Drain #2 — MCP Servers Add Hidden Overhead

Here’s the invisible drain nobody talks about.

Every connected MCP server loads all of its tool definitions into your context window — not once at session start, but on every single message.

In my tests, one MCP server added up to ~18,000 tokens per message, depending on tool definitions.

I ran /context in a completely fresh session — nothing typed, no conversation history. Already down 51,000 tokens from MCP overhead, system prompts, and loaded files.

Before. A. Single. Word.

The fix: Disconnect every MCP server you’re not actively using. If a CLI exists, use the CLI. It’s faster, cheaper, and doesn’t reload on every turn.

Invisible drains are the worst kind. Now you can see them.

Token Drain #3 — Flying Blind Without Visibility Tools

You wouldn’t drive cross-country without a fuel gauge.

But most people run entire Claude Code sessions with zero visibility into where their tokens are going.

/context — shows exactly what's eating your tokens right now. History, MCP overhead, loaded files, everything broken down.

/cost — shows actual token usage and estimated spend for the current session.

Set up a terminal status line showing your model, a usage progress bar, and live token count. Keep your Claude dashboard open in a tab next to your work.

You cannot fix what you cannot see.

Token Drain #4 — Sending Multiple Messages When One Would Do

Three separate messages cost three times what one combined message costs.

Because each new message forces Claude to re-read everything before it.

❌ Instead of this:

  • “Summarize this” → wait
  • “Now extract the key issues” → wait
  • “Now suggest a fix” → wait

✅ Do this:

  • “Summarize this, extract the key issues, and suggest a fix.” → done

And when Claude gets something wrong — don’t send a correction. Edit your original message and regenerate. Corrections stack onto history forever. Edits replace the bad exchange entirely.

One precise message beats three vague ones. Every time.

Token Drain #5 — Letting the Model Go Down the Wrong Path

The single biggest token waste isn’t bad prompts.

It’s Claude confidently going the wrong direction for 20 messages before you notice.

Plan Mode fixes this. It lets Claude map out the full approach, ask clarifying questions, and confirm direction — before writing a single line of code.

Five messages of planning saves forty messages of rebuilding.

Copy this into your CLAUDE.md right now:

Do not make any changes until you have 95% confidence 
in what needs to be built. Ask follow-up questions 
until you reach that confidence level.

The tokens you spend planning are the cheapest tokens in your session.

Token Drain #6 — Bloated Instruction Files

Your CLAUDE.md is read by Claude on every single message. Not once per session.

Every. Single. Message.

A 1,000-line CLAUDE.md means you’re paying for 1,000 lines of context every time you say anything — even “hi.”

The fix: Keep it under 200 lines. Tech stack, coding conventions, build commands, the 95% rule. That’s it.

CLAUDE.md should be an index, not an encyclopedia. Tell Claude where things live — not everything it needs to know. It can look things up when needed. It doesn’t need to carry everything everywhere.

“Every line you cut from CLAUDE.md saves tokens for the rest of your career.”

Token Drain #7 — Waiting Too Long to Compact Context

Claude Code auto-compacts at 95% context capacity.

By the time it kicks in, your context is already severely degraded. There’s a real phenomenon called “lost in the middle” — models pay the most attention to the beginning and end of context, and largely ignore everything in between.

You’re paying full price for context Claude is barely reading.

The fix: Run /compact manually at 60% capacity with specific instructions on what to preserve. Don't wait for the system to rescue you.

After three or four compacts, quality degrades regardless. At that point: get a session summary, /clear, paste the summary back in, continue fresh.

Don’t wait for the system to save you. Save yourself first.

Token Drain #8 — Idle Sessions Killing Cache Efficiency

This one surprises everyone.

Claude Code uses prompt caching to avoid reprocessing unchanged context between messages. It’s automatic and saves you tokens passively.

The cache expires after a short idle window — typically just a few minutes.

Walk away for longer than that — coffee, a call, Twitter — and when you return, your next message reprocesses the entire context window from scratch. Full cost. No discount.

This is why usage randomly spikes after breaks. It’s not random. It’s the cache expiring.

The fix: If you need to step away, run /compact or /clear first. Don't let an idle session become an expensive one.

A short break can cost thousands of tokens. Now you know why.

Token Drain #9 — Running Heavy Tasks at the Wrong Time

Some users report faster session drain during peak platform hours — typically weekday mornings and early afternoons — though this isn’t officially documented by Anthropic.

What is clear: heavy sessions during high-demand periods feel more expensive.

The fix: Schedule big refactors, multi-agent sessions, and large codebase work for off-peak hours — evenings and weekends when platform demand is lower.

And when you’re near a usage reset with budget remaining? Go heavy. Spin up agents. Get your full money’s worth before the clock resets.

Work with the clock, not against it.

Token Drain #10 — Using Expensive Models Where Cheaper Ones Would Do

Not every task needs your most powerful model.

Here’s the hierarchy that saves budget without sacrificing output:

  • Haiku 4.5 — sub-agents, formatting, research summaries, simple lookups. Cheap. Fast. More than enough for 80% of subtasks.
  • Sonnet 4.6 — default for most real coding work. Right choice most of the time.
  • Opus — deep architectural planning only. When Sonnet genuinely wasn’t enough. Keep this rare.

Agent workflows burn 7–10x more tokens than single-agent sessions — each sub-agent wakes with its own full context reload.

The fix: Delegate exploration and research tasks to Haiku 4.5 sub-agents. Return only summarized insights to your main session.

80% of your tokens at Haiku prices instead of Sonnet prices is a completely different economics.

The Mindset Shift That Ties Everything Together

Here’s what nobody says out loud:

Hitting the limit isn’t a failure. If you’re implementing these fixes and still occasionally hitting it — that means you’re shipping something serious. You’re using this tool at the level it was built for.

The goal was never to avoid limits entirely.

The goal is to stop hitting it by accident.

Burning tokens on correction loops, invisible MCP overhead, and 30-message conversations that should have been three — that’s waste.

Burning tokens on real, deep, meaningful work that needed every single one — that’s power.

“Most people don’t need more tokens. They need fewer mistakes.”

You’ve just learned how to make fewer.

Quick-Start Checklist — Do These Right Now

  • [ ] Run /context — see what's eating your tokens before anything else
  • [ ] Run /cost — see your actual session spend
  • [ ] Disconnect every unused MCP server
  • [ ] Set up a terminal status line showing model + usage % + token count
  • [ ] Copy the 95% confidence rule into your CLAUDE.md
  • [ ] Trim CLAUDE.md to under 200 lines
  • [ ] Use /clear between every unrelated task
  • [ ] Set a manual /compact reminder at 60% context
  • [ ] Move heavy sessions to off-peak hours
  • [ ] Batch multi-step instructions into single messages
  • [ ] Stop correcting — edit and regenerate instead

Token architecture and usage limits referenced from Anthropic documentation, GitHub issue tracker, and community reports — April 2026.

You just learned what took me two months and a lot of wasted money to figure out.

Most people will read this, nod, and go back to upgrading their plan.

But you’re still here. All 10 drains. Every fix.

Most people will read this and forget it.
The few who apply it will feel the difference immediately.

Now close this tab, open your terminal, and run /context.

The machine hasn’t changed. But now — neither have you.
